title.en: Beyond AB — Core BC Topics Overview

body.en: Beyond AB — Core BC Topics Overview covers essential College Board AP Calculus BC competencies across foundational mechanics, intermediate analysis, and advanced FRQ problem solving.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Scope of BC-Only Topics & Weighting

body.en: AP Calculus BC introduces 4 major content areas beyond AB: advanced integration, logistic differential equations, parametric/polar/vector functions, and infinite sequences/series.

value.en: Integration by parts, partial fractions, improper integrals
Euler's method, logistic growth differential equations
Parametric curves, 2D vector kinematics, polar area
Convergence tests, Taylor & Maclaurin series, error bounds

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

What percentage of the AP Calculus BC exam score is typically devoted to Unit 10 (Infinite Sequences and Series)?

solution.en: Unit 10 (Infinite Sequences and Series) accounts for approximately 17–18% of the BC exam, making it the highest-weighted single unit on the exam. It virtually always appears as Question 6 on the Free-Response section.

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Algorithmic Comparison: Euler vs Analytic, Series vs Polynomials

body.en: Compare numerical methods (Euler steps) with exact differential solutions and polynomial approximations.

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

In what fundamental way does Euler's Method differ from separation of variables when analyzing a differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\)?

solution.en: Separation of variables finds an exact symbolic closed-form solution \(y(x)\). Euler's Method is a numerical approximation technique that uses local tangent line slopes to step incrementally along the curve.

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — Multi-Topic FRQ Connections & College Board Pitfalls

body.en: Analyze how polar area integrals, improper integrals, and power series coefficients intersect on BC exams.

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

Explain why the improper integral \(\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^p}\,dx\) converges if and only if \(p > 1\), and connect this to the p-series test \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^p}\).

solution.en: By the Integral Test, \(\int_1^M x^{-p}\,dx = \left[ \frac{x^{1-p}}{1-p} \right]_1^M\). As \(M \to \infty\), \(M^{1-p} \to 0\) if and only if the exponent \(1-p < 0 \iff p > 1\). Therefore, both the improper integral and the corresponding p-series converge for \(p > 1\) and diverge for \(p \le 1\).
